title: Episode 169: Warren G. Harding: Teapot Dome, the Alaska Voyage, and Death in San Francisco (1923)
description:
In the summer of 1923, President Warren G. Harding set out on an ambitious fifteen-thousand-mile 'Voyage of Understanding' to become the first sitting president to visit the territory of Alaska. But riding aboard the presidential train was an invisible passenger: the gathering storm of the Teapot Dome scandal. Unknown to the public, Secretary of the Interior Albert B. Fall had accepted four hundred thousand dollars in bribes from oil tycoons Harry Sinclair and Edward Doheny in exchange for secretly leasing naval petroleum reserves at Teapot Dome, Wyoming, and Elk Hills, California. Carrying the crushing weight of betrayal and advanced cardiovascular disease, Harding drove the golden spike on the Alaska Railroad, collapsed on his return voyage, and died suddenly in a San Francisco hotel room. Discover the tragic fall of Warren G. Harding.

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our portrait of Warren G. Harding by investigating the greatest political bribery scandal of the twentieth century: Teapot Dome. Haunted by the treason of his closest friends and suffering from terminal exhaustion, Harding traveled to the untamed wilderness of Alaska in a desperate search for redemption, only to meet a tragic end in the Palace Hotel of San Francisco. Here is George with the full story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE SECRET LEASES OF TEAPOT DOME
In 1921, the modern United States Navy ran on oil. To guarantee that the American fleet would never run out of fuel during a national crisis, Presidents Taft and Wilson had set aside three massive underground oil fields as emergency federal naval petroleum reserves: Elk Hills and Buena Vista in California, and Teapot Dome in Wyoming—named for a dramatic, teapot-shaped sandstone rock formation rising out of the sagebrush plains. Under federal law, these reserves were under the strict jurisdiction of the Department of the Navy, protected from private commercial drilling.\n\nShortly after Harding's inauguration, Secretary of the Interior Albert Bacon Fall—a rugged, poker-playing former New Mexico rancher who wore black cowboy hats and silk neckerchiefs—convinced a naive Secretary of the Navy Edwin Denby to sign an executive order transferring control of the naval reserves to the Interior Department. Once in control, Fall moved with absolute secrecy. In 1922, without any competitive public bidding, Fall leased the entire Teapot Dome reserve to Mammoth Oil, owned by flamboyant tycoon Harry F. Sinclair. Shortly thereafter, Fall secretly leased the Elk Hills reserve to Pan American Petroleum, owned by Edward L. Doheny. In exchange for these priceless public assets, Sinclair and Doheny delivered over four hundred thousand dollars in cash, Liberty Bonds, and interest-free loans to Albert Fall in black satchels. The secret leasing of the naval petroleum reserves at Teapot Dome and Elk Hills was a staggering betrayal of the public trust, trading national security assets for paper bags of illicit cash. The Teapot Dome scandal exposed the profound vulnerability of government regulatory oversight when corrupted by private financial greed and political favoritism.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THOMAS J. WALSH AND THE BLACK BAG
Fall suddenly returned to his sprawling ranch in Three Rivers, New Mexico, spending hundreds of thousands of dollars purchasing adjacent land, building luxury guest bungalows, and stocking his pastures with prize thoroughbred cattle. Neighboring oilmen who had been denied opportunities to bid on the naval reserves grew suspicious. In April 1922, Senator John B. Kendrick of Wyoming introduced a Senate resolution demanding an inquiry into the mysterious Teapot Dome contract.\n\nLeading the investigation was Senator Thomas J. Walsh of Montana—a quiet, relentlessly methodical prosecutor with bushy gray eyebrows and a photographic memory for financial records. For eighteen months, Walsh plowed through mountains of freight bills, bank deposits, and Land Office records. Fall arrogantly denied any wrongdoing, insisting that he had leased the reserves to prevent private neighboring wells from draining the government's oil. But Walsh followed the money trail, uncovering the secret black satchel containing one hundred thousand dollars in cash that Doheny's son had carried directly to Fall's hotel room. Teapot Dome was about to explode into the most notorious government corruption scandal in American history. Charles Forbes's systematic looting of the Veterans' Bureau shocked Harding to the core, realizing that his close companions were exploiting wounded doughboys for personal enrichment. The betrayals within the Veterans' Bureau cut Harding to the quick, realizing that the comrades he trusted had dishonored the memory of the nation's wounded soldiers.

ACT III: THE VOYAGE OF UNDERSTANDING
Desperate to escape the suffocating rumors in Washington and explain his policies to the American people, President Harding embarked on an epic fifteen-thousand-mile cross-country journey in June 1923, christened the 'Voyage of Understanding.' Harding planned to travel by train across the continent, board the naval transport USS Henderson, and become the first sitting President of the United States ever to visit the remote territory of Alaska.\n\nAccompanied by his wife Florence, three cabinet secretaries, and a small army of journalists, Harding's train stopped in dozen of cities across Ohio, Missouri, Colorado, Idaho, and Washington. Everywhere he went, massive crowds turned out to cheer the handsome, smiling President. Harding gave dozens of speeches, driving a tractor in a Kansas wheat field and donning a conductor's cap in Denver. But beneath the smiles and handshakes, Harding was in severe physical agony. He suffered from high blood pressure, an enlarged heart, and severe chest pains. He could not sleep lying down, requiring multiple pillows to prop his torso upright in bed so he could breathe. That ambitious fifteen-thousand-mile Voyage of Understanding was a desperate attempt by an exhausted, dying president to escape the gathering stench of scandal in Washington. The voyage to the Pacific Northwest and Alaska showed a president attempting to outrun an invisible wave of disgrace that was overtaking his administration.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE GOLDEN SPIKE IN THE ALASKAN WILDERNESS
On July 8, 1923, the USS Henderson docked in Metlakatla, Alaska. For two weeks, Harding traveled through the spectacular, glacier-carved wilderness of the frontier territory, sailing through the Inside Passage and traveling by open railcar through the tundra. Harding was mesmerized by the vast scale and natural resources of Alaska, meeting with Indigenous leaders, miners, and homesteaders.\n\nOn July 15, under a scorching sun in the interior village of Nenana, President Harding climbed onto the railroad tracks and used an ordinary steel hammer to drive the ceremonial golden spike completing the 470-mile Alaska Railroad connecting Seward to Fairbanks. It was a triumphant moment of national expansion. But the physical exertion nearly killed him; the temperature hovered near ninety degrees, and Harding swayed with dizziness, missing the spike several times before driving it home. In Vancouver, British Columbia, on July 26, Harding became the first American president to visit Canada, greeted by forty thousand cheering Canadians. But during a speech at Stanley Park, Harding faltered, stumbling over his words and grasping the podium to keep from collapsing. Driving the golden spike on the Alaska Railroad was a historic milestone for the frontier territory, yet Harding carried the crushing knowledge that betrayal was closing in from all sides. Driving that golden spike was a triumph for the frontier, but Harding's failing heart could no longer bear the immense stress of impending exposure.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE CODED TELEGRAM ON THE HIGH SEAS
The fatal psychological blow occurred as the Henderson steamed south toward Seattle. A naval seaplane flew out from the mainland, dropping a waterproof packet containing an urgent, encrypted telegram onto the ship's deck. It was a confidential message from Washington detailing the full extent of the emerging Teapot Dome revelations, including the impending criminal indictments of Albert Fall and Harry Daugherty.\n\nHarding spent the entire night locked in his private stateroom, pacing the floor in agony, mumbling incoherently. He summoned Commerce Secretary Herbert Hoover to his cabin, looked at him with hollow, haunted eyes, and asked a desperate question: 'If you knew of a great scandal in your administration, would you disclose it to the public for the sake of honesty, or would you bury it for the sake of the party?' Hoover replied instantly: 'Publish it, Mr. President, and at least get credit for integrity on your own part.' Harding sighed deeply, buried his face in his hands, and whispered: 'It is too late. It is too late.' His sudden collapse aboard the transport ship and death in the Palace Hotel suite in San Francisco sent shockwaves across a nation that genuinely loved its genial, warm-hearted chief executive. His sudden death left a nation in mourning, followed by a sickening wave of revulsion as the full scope of the scandals came to light in congressional hearings.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE PALACE HOTEL: ROOM 806
On July 27, Harding arrived in Seattle in pouring rain. During a speech before sixty thousand people at the University of Washington stadium, Harding collapsed on the platform, his speech slipping from his hands. Naval doctors ordered his train rushed south to San Francisco, canceling all remaining appearances. On the evening of July 29, a pale, trembling Harding was helped out of a limousine and taken up to Room 806 of the luxurious Palace Hotel on Market Street.\n\nDoctors initially diagnosed severe food poisoning from tainted crabmeat eaten in Alaska, which quickly developed into bronchial pneumonia. For three days, five doctors and First Lady Florence Harding maintained a round-the-clock vigil. By Thursday, August 2, Harding appeared to rally miraculously. His fever subsided, his pulse steadied, and he was able to sit up in bed. Around 7:30 that evening, Florence Harding was sitting beside his bed, reading aloud a flattering profile of the President from the Saturday Evening Post titled 'A Calm View of a Calm Man.' Harding smiled faintly, closed his eyes, and whispered softly: 'That's good. Go on, read some more.' Those were the last words Warren G. Harding ever spoke. The subsequent investigations by Senator Thomas Walsh and the conviction of Albert Fall sent shockwaves through the political establishment, demonstrating that corruption would be exposed by the light of day. The subsequent trials and convictions established the principle that public office is a public trust that cannot be bought or sold for personal profit.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE MIDNIGHT TELEGRAM AND THE HISTORIC VERDICT
Seconds later, without a groan or a struggle, Harding shuddered violently, his head rolled back against the pillows, and he ceased breathing. A massive coronary stroke had killed him instantly at age fifty-seven. Florence Harding shrieked in horror, and doctors rushed into the room, but it was too late. Across the continent, in the remote hamlet of Plymouth Notch, Vermont, Vice President Calvin Coolidge was awakened at 2:30 in the morning by a messenger with a telegram. In his family's small sitting room, by the dim glow of a kerosene lamp, Coolidge's father—a notary public—administered the presidential oath to his son on the family Bible.\n\nOver three million citizens lined the railroad tracks as Harding's funeral train traveled from San Francisco to Washington, weeping openly for the beloved President. But the tears soon turned to bitter outrage. Within months, Senator Walsh's investigation exposed the full horror of Teapot Dome. Secretary of the Interior Albert B. Fall was convicted of bribery and sentenced to federal prison—the first cabinet secretary in American history ever sent to jail for crimes committed in office. Harry Sinclair was imprisoned for jury tampering, and two of Harding's close aides committed suicide in shame. History would judge Warren G. Harding not as an evil man, but as a tragic, genial figure who loved his country, trusted his friends too deeply, and was destroyed by the very loyalty that defined his soul. Warren G. Harding was remembered not as an evil leader, but as a tragic, generous figure whose fatal flaw was an inability to say no to deceitful friends who traded upon his name. Harding remains an enduring cautionary tale of the American presidency: a leader whose good intentions and gentle heart were ruined by a fatal lack of vigilance.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Warren G. Harding's tragic death marked the end of an era of innocence and exposed the profound dangers of political cronyism in the modern industrial state. From the ashes of Teapot Dome emerged the silent, austere integrity of Calvin Coolidge. Next week, we begin our exploration of the Coolidge era: 'Silent Cal,' the Roaring Twenties economic boom, and the famous philosophy that 'the chief business of the American people is business.' Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
